analysis.one_liner: Requires union representation elections to wait at least 35 days and blocks small-group bargaining units.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 235-188 on November 30, 2011, with 229 of 241 Republicans voting yes, but the Senate never brought it to a vote and it died on the Senate calendar when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act to guarantee employers at least 35 days between a union election petition and the vote, add a required pre-election hearing of at least 14 days, and overturn a 2011 labor board decision that allowed small groups of workers — such as nursing home aides — to form their own bargaining units. In practice, it would give employers a longer window to campaign against a union before workers vote, and would make it harder for small groups of employees to organize on their own. It also requires employers to hand over a list of eligible voters with contact information to all parties, a provision that helps union organizers reach workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing union organizing campaigns gain the most: a guaranteed five-week minimum before any election vote, plus a required pre-election hearing, extends the period in which they can hold meetings and make their case to employees. The bill also shields employers from the small 'micro' bargaining units the labor board had begun approving, which would otherwise let small groups of workers unionize a segment of a workplace. The voter-list requirement modestly benefits union organizers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the labor board to schedule any union election no sooner than 35 calendar days after a petition is filed, guaranteeing a longer window before workers vote
Requires a pre-election hearing at least 14 days after a petition is filed, adding a mandatory procedural step before any election

Reverses the labor board's Specialty Healthcare decision by requiring bargaining units to share a 'sufficient community of interest' and barring exclusion of employees unless their interests are genuinely distinct, which blocks small workplace-segment units
Requires the employer to provide a list of all eligible voters, with a chosen form of contact information, to all parties in the election

analysis.who_pays: Workers seeking to form a union bear the cost: they must wait at least 35 days to vote, during which employers can hold mandatory meetings and campaign against the union while the union has no comparable access. Workers in small, distinct groups lose the micro-unit path the labor board had opened, leaving them to bargain in larger units or not at all. The modest countervailing benefit is guaranteed access to the voter contact list.

drawbacks.text: Workers who file an election petition must wait at least 35 days before voting; that waiting period is one employers can use to hold mandatory meetings and press employees against unionizing, while union organizers lack equal access to workers

By barring small-group bargaining units, the bill closes off organizing for narrow groups of employees — such as nursing aides or a single department — whose interests may differ from the wider workforce

Backers would answer that a minimum window gives employees adequate time to hear both sides before voting, and that the community-of-interest standard prevents fragmented units that split co-workers against each other; the bill's one pro-worker element is requiring employers to release a voter contact list to all parties

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's headline effects run almost entirely to employers: a guaranteed delay before union votes and the elimination of micro-units. Its one provision favoring workers — the voter list with contact information — is small by comparison. The partisan name ('Workforce Democracy and Fairness Act') does not match the substance, which narrows workers' access to quicker elections and smaller units. As designed, it would mainly serve employers resisting organizing campaigns; it never became law.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a near party-line vote, but the Senate, then run by Democrats, placed it on the calendar without ever bringing it to a vote, and it died there when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 5, 2011, and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which held a hearing on October 12 and a markup on October 26 before reporting it amended on November 10
The House took it up on November 30, 2011, defeating four Democratic amendments and a Democratic motion to recommit (185-239) before passing it 235-188
Final passage split almost entirely by party: 229 of 241 Republicans voted yes while 180 of 192 Democrats voted no
The Senate received the bill on December 1, 2011, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar on December 16, 2011 — no vote was ever held before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced faster union elections and small micro-bargaining units are better off: the bill died without a Senate vote, so the labor board's Specialty Healthcare standard and the existing election timing stayed in place for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 229 of 241 Republicans voted yes while 180 of 192 Democrats voted no; every Democratic floor amendment and the motion to recommit also failed on party lines.

industries.industry: Employers facing union organizing campaigns (healthcare chains, nursing homes, manufacturers, service employers)
industries.note: The bill guarantees them at least 35 days before a union vote — a window in which they can hold mandatory meetings and campaign against organizing — and blocks the micro-units that would have let small worker groups organize segments of their workplaces. Its interest in this bill ran against workers' access to quicker elections.

Slower elections and the closure of the micro-unit path would cost unions elections and members, particularly among small distinct worker groups. The voter-contact-list provision is the one element that would have helped them reach workers.
